final_task_tree.title: Figure out a training plan for my dog
final_task_tree.description:
Rescue border collie mix, 14 months. Pulls hard on the leash and barks at every other dog on walks. South Bay, California; I can do evenings and weekends.

Three things only:
1. Whether to hire a trainer or do it myself.
2. If hiring — two or three local options with real prices.
3. A week-by-week plan for the first four weeks.

Don't research anything beyond those three.

comments.body:
Done — report attached, tree built out. Answers to your three questions:

**1. Hire or DIY → hybrid.** The pulling is pure DIY, no reason to pay for it. The barking at dogs is where you want a couple of hours of professional eyes, because the two things owners reliably get wrong (threshold distance, and reward timing) are things you can't see in yourself. Buy a small amount of expertise, not a big package.

**2. Trainers →** Orion Dog Training, San Jose has the best fit *and* a published price: **$395** for a 6-week in-person reactive-dog class, capped at 4–5 teams, curriculum is literally the same toolkit as the plan below. They do a free 20-min phone consult. D For Dogz in Palo Alto runs a comparable "Growly Dog" class but doesn't publish a price, so there's a call subtask to get one. Stacy's Wag'n Train and Zoom Room Santa Clara are listed as fallbacks.

**3. Weeks 1–4 →** four subtasks, one per week, each with the daily/weekend sessions spelled out. Shape: week 1 mechanics with zero dog encounters, week 2 find his threshold and pay him for seeing dogs, week 3 he starts disengaging on his own + emergency U-turn, week 4 combine and review. Two rules do most of the work: tight leash never earns forward progress, and never let him rehearse a full reaction.

Two things I'd flag as the highest-leverage items in the whole tree: **buy a front-clip harness before week 1**, and **run the frustration-vs-fear diagnostic** (subtask has the body-language checklist). At 14 months he's likely a frustrated greeter rather than a fearful dog, and which one he is changes the long-term plan — every trainer will ask you first thing.

Status → needs_review. Five human subtasks sitting under this task: buy gear, run the diagnostic, two calls, then book. Nothing is blocked on me.

report.markdown:
﻿# Training plan — 14-month rescue border collie mix, South Bay CA

Pulling on leash + barking at every dog. Three answers, nothing else.

---

## 1. Hire or DIY?

**Hybrid. Book 2–4 sessions (or one small reactive-dog class) with a reactivity-experienced trainer, and do the daily practice yourself. Don't go pure DIY, and don't buy a big multi-week package up front.**

The two problems in the brief are not the same kind of problem:

| Problem | What it actually is | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Pulling hard on leash | A mechanics and skills problem. Clear protocols, easy to self-teach, mostly about your consistency. | **DIY.** You do not need to pay anyone for this. |
| Barking at every dog | An emotional / arousal problem. Depends on reading body language and getting distance and timing right. | **Get eyes on it.** This is where owners consistently go wrong. |

The specific thing a professional buys you: **the two most common owner errors in reactivity work are misjudging threshold distance (working too close, so the dog can't learn) and mistiming the reward (marking after the reaction instead of before).** Both are things you cannot see in yourself. One or two sessions of somebody watching you walk your actual dog fixes both, and after that the daily work is yours.

Second reason to get a professional look: at 14 months he's a textbook adolescent, and adolescent dogs who bark at every dog on leash split into **frustrated greeters** (wants to get there, leash is in the way) and **fear-based reactors** (wants the dog to go away). They look similar from across the street and the long-term plan diverges — the frustrated dog eventually earns controlled greetings, the fearful one never gets pushed into them. Getting this wrong costs months. A pro calls it in one session. (There's a subtask with the body-language checklist so you can take a first stab at it yourself before you call.)

**Why not a big package up front:** you have no data yet on how he responds. Buy a small amount of expertise, run the plan for four weeks, then decide with numbers in hand.

**Escalate beyond this plan if:** he air-snaps or bites another dog, or the numbers in your log are flat after four honest weeks. That's a vet check plus a veterinary behaviourist referral, not more of the same.

---

## 2. Local options, with real prices

Prices checked on the providers' own pages, August 2026.

### Option A — Orion Dog Training, San Jose · **$395** · recommended

| | |
|---|---|
| Programme | "My dog is reactive, now what?" — 6-week in-person small-group class for reactive dogs |
| Price | **$395** (published) |
| Format | ~3,000 sq ft indoor facility, capped at **4–5 dog/handler teams**, homework with video explanations, whole family welcome |
| Curriculum | Emergency U-turn · "Look at That" · Catch 1-2-3 pattern game · Up & Down |
| Also | **Free 20-minute phone consult**; keeps a network of force-free certified trainers for referrals |

This is the best fit of anything found. The curriculum is line-for-line the toolkit your 4-week plan uses, the price is real and published rather than "contact us", and the 4–5 team cap in a large indoor room is the thing that makes a class survivable for a reactive dog — most group classes pack dogs too close together and you spend six weeks over threshold.

### Option B — D For Dogz (D For Dog Training), Palo Alto / San Jose · price on call

Runs a **"Growly Dog Foundations" / Leash Reactive Dog Foundations** group class in Palo Alto, plus dedicated leash-reactive private training. Free intro call. No published price — that's the point of the call subtask. Worth getting as your comparison quote because the programme is explicitly built for reactive dogs rather than being general obedience with reactivity bolted on.

### Option C — fallbacks if the first two don't fit your schedule

- **Stacy's Wag'n Train, San Jose** — 25+ years, private lessons and behaviour packages. Their fees page didn't load; you'd have to ask.
- **Zoom Room Santa Clara** — publishes a full price page for private sessions, classes and memberships. Chain-model, general training rather than reactivity specialists; use as a price benchmark or if you want something walkable-to on a weeknight.

**Suggested sequence:** free Orion consult → D For Dogz quote → book. Two calls, then decide. Don't book off the first call.

---

## 3. Weeks 1–4

Full detail is in the four week-subtasks. The shape of it:

| Week | Focus | Daily | Weekend |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | Mechanics only, **zero** dog encounters | 2 × 10 min "red light / green light" in a boring place; 2 min of 1-2-3 game indoors | 2 sniffaris; run the frustration-vs-fear diagnostic |
| **2** | Find threshold distance; Engage-Disengage **level 1** (pay him for *seeing* a dog) | Leash work + penalty yards | 3–4 × 10 min threshold sessions |
| **3** | Engage-Disengage **level 2** (he looks away on his own); teach emergency U-turn | Leash work on mildly distracting routes; 2 min U-turn game | 4 × 10 min sessions; 1-2-3 as dogs pass |
| **4** | Combine on real walks; review the numbers | Normal walks with the two rules | 2 parallel-walk sessions; end-of-week review and decision |

Sniffaris run 3× a week throughout — they are load-bearing, not filler.

**The five rules underneath it:**

1. **Split the walks in two, permanently.** *Training* walks are 10–15 min, short, boring, no other dogs. *Decompression* walks are on a long line, he picks the route, he sniffs as long as he wants, you ask for nothing. Sniffing gives a herding brain a job that competes with scanning for threats, which is why it lowers reactivity without you correcting anything.
2. **Leash: tight leash never earns forward progress.** The instant it tightens you stop dead — no yanking, no talking. He turns back, leash loosens, you mark and move. Add penalty yards (back up a few steps) when he's locked forward. Standard positive-reinforcement practice, and the whole method is that one rule applied without exception.
3. **Reactivity: Engage-Disengage, in two levels.** Level 1 — he looks at the dog, you mark and treat. You are paying him purely for noticing. Level 2 — he looks at the dog, you wait 3–5 seconds, and the moment he looks away *on his own* you mark and treat. **3–5 clean reps at one distance before you close any distance.** If he can't disengage within 5 seconds, you're too close: add distance, drop to level 1.
4. **1-2-3 is your emergency tool.** Count "one, two, three" out loud in a steady rhythm; the treat lands beside your leg on "three", every time, regardless of what he did. Teach it at home so it's a reflex, then use it while a dog goes past. It gives him a predictable structure to hold instead of a decision to make.
5. **Never rehearse the reaction.** Dog too close? U-turn, cross the street, step behind a parked car. Every full bark-lunge is a rep of the wrong behaviour. And reactions stack across a day — after a bad one, take a rest day: quiet route, no training asks, calming enrichment, more sleep. Recovery is part of the protocol.

**Gear:** front-clip harness, 6 ft leash, 15–30 ft long line, treat pouch, and two tiers of treats — ordinary ones for leash work, high-value (chicken, cheese, liver) reserved *only* for dog-sighting work. **No prong, no e-collar, no choke chain, no retractable leash** — adding pain at the exact moment he sees another dog teaches him that other dogs mean pain.

**Measure two numbers, one line per walk:** full reactions per walk, and the closest distance at which he saw a dog and recovered. Expect the distance to improve before the count does. Those two numbers are also what decides, at the end of week 4, whether you keep going solo or escalate.

---

## Your next five moves

1. Buy the gear (30 min, before week 1).
2. Book the free Orion consult — https://www.oriondogtraining.com/reactivedog
3. Call D For Dogz for a comparison quote and a start date.
4. Pick one and book it.
5. Start week 1 now — don't wait for a class start date.

subtasks.title: Decide: DIY vs. hire a trainer for leash pulling + dog reactivity
subtasks.description:
Question 1 of the brief. FINDING / RECOMMENDATION:

**Hybrid: 2-4 private sessions with a reactivity-experienced trainer, then DIY the daily practice.** Do NOT go pure DIY, and do NOT buy a big multi-week package yet.

Why not pure DIY:
- Two problems are tangled together. Pulling is a mechanics/skills problem you can absolutely fix yourself. Barking at every dog is an emotional/arousal problem, and getting the distance ("threshold") and timing right is the part owners consistently get wrong on their own. AKC's guidance on on-leash lunging at other dogs is to get help from a trainer with specific leash-reactivity experience.
- The usual DIY failure mode is practising too close to other dogs, so the dog rehearses the reaction instead of unlearning it. A trainer watching you for one hour catches this immediately.
- Common advice threshold: get a pro if the behaviour is hurting your quality of life, or if your own attempts aren't producing visible change within a few weeks. "Barks at EVERY other dog" at 14 months is already past the first bar.

Why not a big package either:
- At 14 months this is textbook adolescent reactivity, and the most likely subtype for a border collie mix that is a rescue is FRUSTRATION (frustrated greeter — wants to get to the dog) rather than FEAR (wants the dog to go away). Frustration cases usually respond fast once the owner gets the mechanics and threshold right. You may not need 6-8 sessions.
- The daily reps are the actual treatment, and only you can do those. A trainer cannot walk your dog for you.

Diagnostic the owner should run before/at the first session — it changes the plan:
- Does he play fine with dogs OFF leash, and is his body forward/tail high/whining-barking to get closer? → frustration. Better prognosis, mostly impulse control + leash mechanics.
- Is he trying to back away, hackles up, barking to make the dog leave, stiff or freezing first? → fear. Slower, needs more careful desensitisation, and worth asking about a vet/veterinary-behaviourist consult.

Format guidance found: private training first for dogs that bark/lunge, because they need controlled distance and a threshold-based setup; group classes are cheaper per session but only appropriate once the dog can actually think near other dogs — or if the class is specifically a "reactive dog" class where distance and barriers are managed. So: private first, then optionally a reactive-dog group class as step 2.

Avoid: any trainer selling prong/e-collar as the fix for reactivity, and any board-and-train — the problem happens on YOUR walks with YOU holding the leash.

subtasks.title: Write the week-by-week plan for weeks 1-4
subtasks.description:
Question 3 of the brief. FINDINGS — the plan is built and split into four child subtasks (one per week) so you can tick them off. Summary of the design below; full detail is in the report and in each week's subtask.

DESIGN PRINCIPLES USED:
1. Separate the two problems. Loose-leash walking is trained in BORING places with NO other dogs. Reactivity is worked at a distance where the dog can still eat and think. Never train both at once in week 1-2 — that's the classic mistake.
2. Split walks into two types, permanently: (a) TRAINING walks, 10-15 min, short, boring, in your control; (b) DECOMPRESSION / "sniffari" walks — long line, dog picks the route, dog sniffs as much as he wants, no obedience asked. Sniffing lowers arousal and gives a herding brain a competing job instead of scanning for triggers. Aim for at least 3 sniffaris a week.
3. Leash mechanics = "red light / green light": the instant the leash goes tight you stop dead, no yanking. When he turns back and the leash loosens, mark and move on. Tight leash never earns forward progress. Add "penalty yards" (back up a few steps) when he's locked forward on something. Both endorsed as standard positive-reinforcement approaches.
4. Reactivity = Engage-Disengage (a.k.a. "Look at That"). Level 1: he looks at the dog → you mark → he gets the treat. Level 2 (once level 1 is solid): he looks at the dog, you WAIT 3-5 seconds for him to look away on his own → mark → treat. Rule: 3-5 clean reps at one distance before you close the distance at all. If he can't look away within 5 seconds, you're too close — go back to level 1 and add distance.
5. Pattern games as the emergency tool. The 1-2-3 game (from Leslie McDevitt's Control Unleashed): count "one, two, three" out loud in a steady rhythm and the treat is delivered at "three" beside your leg, every time regardless of what he did. It gives the dog a predictable structure to hold onto while a trigger goes past. Teach it at home first so it works when you need it.
6. Manage trigger stacking. Reactions are cumulative across a day. After a bad encounter, take a rest day: quiet route, no training asks, calming enrichment, extra sleep. Rest is part of the protocol, not a break from it.
7. Never rehearse the reaction. If a dog appears too close, you bail — U-turn, cross the street, go behind a parked car. Every full-blown bark-lunge is a rep of the wrong behaviour.

GEAR (buy before week 1): front-clip harness (reduces lunging leverage without hurting the neck), a 6 ft leash for training walks, a 15-30 ft long line for sniffaris, a treat pouch, and two tiers of treats — ordinary kibble/biscuits for leash work, high-value (chicken, cheese, hot dog, freeze-dried liver) reserved ONLY for dog-sighting work. No prong collar, no e-collar, no choke chain, no retractable leash.

SUCCESS MEASURE — keep a one-line log per walk: number of full reactions (barking/lunging), and the closest distance he managed to see a dog and recover. Those two numbers are what tells you whether week 4 is better than week 1. Expect the distance number to improve before the reaction count does.

subtasks.title: Week 1 — foundations only, zero dog encounters
subtasks.description:
GOAL: teach the mechanics with no triggers present. You are not fixing reactivity this week.

DAILY (10-15 min, evenings):
- Loose-leash 'red light / green light' in the most boring place you can find: your driveway, an empty parking lot, a quiet cul-de-sac at dusk. Walk; the instant the leash tightens, stop dead. Don't pull back, don't say anything. Wait. When he turns to you and the leash loosens, mark ('yes') and walk on. That's the whole exercise. 2 x 10 min a day beats 1 x 20.
- 2 minutes of the 1-2-3 pattern game indoors: count 'one, two, three' out loud in a steady rhythm, treat delivered at 'three' next to your leg, every single time no matter what he's doing. Do 10 reps. You are building a reflex, not testing him.

WEEKEND:
- Two decompression sniffaris on the long line, 30-45 min, somewhere with few dogs (industrial street, school grounds after hours, quiet park edge). He picks the direction, he sniffs as long as he likes, you ask for nothing.
- Run the frustration-vs-fear diagnostic (see the sibling task) and write down the answer.

MANAGEMENT RULE all week: if a dog appears, you leave. U-turn, cross the street, duck behind a car. No exceptions. Zero reactions this week is the target.

READY TO MOVE ON WHEN: he offers a loose leash within a few seconds of you stopping, most of the time, in a quiet place; and he snaps his head toward you at 'three' without you cueing anything else.

subtasks.title: Week 2 — find his threshold distance and start Engage-Disengage level 1
subtasks.description:
GOAL: find out how far away another dog has to be for him to still eat and think, and start paying him for looking.

FINDING THE THRESHOLD (do this first, one weekend session): park yourself somewhere you can see dogs at a long distance but never have to pass one — a bench across the street from a park entrance, a parking lot overlooking a trail head. Start absurdly far, 100+ feet. Feed him high-value treats. If he takes food calmly and can look away, that's inside threshold. Move 10 feet closer and retest. The distance where he stops taking food or locks on and stiffens is his threshold — his working distance is 10-15 feet FURTHER BACK than that. Write the number down.

ENGAGE-DISENGAGE LEVEL 1 (3-4 sessions this week, 10 min max each, at the threshold distance):
- He notices the dog → you immediately mark ('yes') → high-value treat. That's it. You are paying him just for SEEING a dog. Don't ask for anything.
- 3-5 clean reps at one distance, then stop. Do not close the distance this week.
- Use the high-value treats you reserved for this and nothing else.

KEEP RUNNING: daily 10-15 min loose-leash red-light/green-light in boring places, and add penalty yards — if he's locked forward and pulling toward something, back up a few steps so pulling literally loses him ground. Plus 3 sniffaris.

STILL BAIL from any close encounter. Still no passing dogs on the sidewalk.

READY TO MOVE ON WHEN: at his threshold distance he reliably takes food, and he's starting to look at you after spotting a dog without being asked.

LOG: reactions per walk, and his threshold distance in feet.

subtasks.title: Week 3 — Engage-Disengage level 2 plus the emergency U-turn
subtasks.description:
GOAL: he starts choosing to look away from dogs on his own, and you get a reliable escape hatch.

ENGAGE-DISENGAGE LEVEL 2 (4 sessions, 10 min each, same threshold distance you established in week 2):
- He notices the dog → you say nothing and WAIT 3-5 seconds → the moment he looks away from the dog on his own, mark and treat.
- If he can't look away within 5 seconds, you are too close. Add distance and drop back to level 1 for that session. No shame in it, this is the whole skill.
- Only after 3-5 clean level-2 reps at one distance do you move 5-10 feet closer. Small increments. If it falls apart, you went too fast — back up.

TEACH THE EMERGENCY U-TURN (2 min a day, no dogs present): pick a phrase like 'let's go!', say it in a bright voice, spin 180 degrees and jog 5 steps away, then treat. Make it a fun game with no trigger attached, so that when you need it in a real ambush it works. Practise 5 reps a session until he turns with you without leash pressure.

ADD 1-2-3 ON WALKS: start using the 1-2-3 game while a dog passes at a comfortable distance, instead of asking him to sit and stare at you. The rhythm gives him something predictable to do while the trigger goes by.

KEEP RUNNING: loose-leash work but now on real short walks with mild distractions (parked cars, people, smells) — still avoid dog-heavy routes. 3 sniffaris.

MANAGE TRIGGER STACKING: after any full reaction, take the next day as a rest day — quiet route, no training asks, calming enrichment (snuffle mat, scatter feed, a chew), extra sleep.

READY TO MOVE ON WHEN: he disengages from a dog on his own within a few seconds at his working distance, and turns with you on the U-turn cue.

subtasks.title: Week 4 — combine the skills on real walks and review the numbers
subtasks.description:
GOAL: put leash mechanics and disengagement together on the routes you actually use, and decide what happens next.

SESSIONS (4-5 this week):
- Two 'parallel walk' style sessions: work in a place with predictable dog traffic (across the street from a park path) and just walk back and forth at your working distance, running 1-2-3 and engage-disengage as dogs come and go. Keep sessions to 15 minutes — quality over duration.
- Two normal neighbourhood walks where the only rules are: leash goes tight, you stop; dog appears, you U-turn or step behind a car and feed. You are not trying to pass dogs at close range yet. Passing at close range is a month 2-3 goal, not a week 4 goal.
- Keep 3 sniffaris. They are not optional — they are what keeps his baseline arousal down.

GRADUALLY SHRINK DISTANCE, not on a schedule but on evidence: only move closer when the previous distance is boring to him.

END-OF-WEEK REVIEW (30 min, sit down with your log):
- Compare week 1 vs week 4: reactions per walk, and closest distance he can see a dog and recover. Distance usually improves before frequency does.
- If the numbers are clearly moving: keep going solo for another 4 weeks, and consider a reactive-dog class as reinforcement.
- If the numbers are flat or worse: stop self-directing and get eyes on it. Book the class or a private session (see the trainer options task). Flat progress after 4 honest weeks is exactly the trigger point trainers name for getting help.
- If he ever escalates to a bite or an air-snap at another dog: stop the DIY plan, and get a vet check plus a referral to a veterinary behaviourist. That changes the category of problem.

READY TO MOVE ON WHEN: you have written the two numbers down and made the keep-going / get-help call.

subtasks.title: Buy the gear before Week 1 starts
subtasks.description:
Shopping list, all of it available at any pet store or online:
- Front-clip (no-pull) harness, fitted — reduces lunging leverage without putting pressure on the neck. This is the single most useful purchase.
- 6 ft flat leash for training walks.
- 15-30 ft long line for decompression sniffaris (a biothane one is easier on the hands than nylon).
- Treat pouch that clips to your waist — fumbling in a pocket loses you the 2-second window that makes marking work.
- Tier 1 treats: plain kibble or small biscuits, for leash mechanics.
- Tier 2 treats: chicken, cheese, hot dog, or freeze-dried liver. These are ONLY used when another dog is in sight, so the dog's appearance predicts the best thing that happens all day.

Do NOT buy: prong collar, e-collar, choke chain, or a retractable leash. All of them either add pain to the exact moment he sees a dog (which makes reactivity worse, not better) or make leash mechanics impossible to teach.

subtasks.title: Run the frustration-vs-fear diagnostic on your first weekend walk
subtasks.description:
Five minutes of watching, and it changes which advice applies to you. Adolescent dogs (12-18 months) with this exact profile split into two camps and they look similar from a distance.

Stand somewhere you can see a dog 60-100 ft away and watch his body:

FRUSTRATED GREETER (very common in adolescent herding mixes): body leaning FORWARD, tail high and often wagging fast, weight on the front feet, whining or squeaking mixed in with the barking, and if he actually gets to the dog he's friendly or over-the-top playful. He wants to get there and the leash is in the way.

FEAR-BASED: body leaning BACK or braced, weight shifted to the rear, tail low or tucked, hackles up, hard stare, closed tight mouth, lip lift, may bark and then retreat. He wants the dog to go away.

Write down which one he looks like and note the specific body signals you saw. Both camps use the same week 1-4 protocol, but the frustrated version usually improves faster and eventually gets controlled greetings as a reward, while the fear version needs slower distance work and never gets pushed into greetings. Tell whichever trainer you talk to what you observed — it's the first thing they'll ask.

subtasks.title: Book the free 20-min phone consult with Orion Dog Training
subtasks.description:
Orion Dog Training, San Jose — offers a free 20-minute phone consultation. Book it via https://www.oriondogtraining.com/reactivedog (their reactive-dog page has the booking link and the class details).

Why them: their 'My dog is reactive, now what?' course is a 6-week in-person small-group class specifically for reactive dogs, $395, capped at 4-5 dog/handler teams in a ~3,000 sq ft indoor facility, with homework and video explanations. The curriculum is emergency U-turn, 'Look at That', the Catch 1-2-3 pattern game and Up & Down — which is exactly the toolkit in your 4-week plan.

Ask on the call:
1. Next start date and day/time — confirm it fits evenings or weekends.
2. Is a 14-month adolescent border collie mix who barks at every dog on leash a fit for the group class, or would they start with privates? (Describe what you saw in the frustration-vs-fear diagnostic.)
3. What's the price of 2-3 private sessions instead, and can privates be credited toward the class later?
4. How much space is there between teams in the room — i.e. can your dog stay under threshold inside the class?
5. What's included in the $395: number of sessions, session length, materials, any follow-up.

Write the answers into this description when you've made the call.

subtasks.title: Call D For Dogz for a second quote and a start date
subtasks.description:
Second option, for comparison — don't book the first one you call.

D For Dogz / D For Dog Training. They run a 'Growly Dog Foundations' / leash-reactive group class in Palo Alto and also do leash-reactive private training. They offer a free intro call.
Pages: https://dfordogtraining.com/private-dog-training-silicon-valley/leash-reactive-dog-private-training/ and https://dfordogtraining.com/dog-training-san-jose/

They do not publish a flat price for the reactive programme, so the point of this call is to get a number. Ask:
1. Exact price of the Growly Dog / leash-reactive group class, number of weeks, session length, location and start date.
2. Exact price of a single private leash-reactivity session, and of their smallest package.
3. Do they use any aversive tools (prong, e-collar, slip lead)? You want a straight no. If the answer is anything other than no, cross them off.
4. Certifications of the actual trainer who'd work with you (CPDT-KA, KPA-CTP, IAABC, CBCC-KA are the ones that mean something).

Write the price and start date into this description after the call.

subtasks.title: Pick one and book it
subtasks.description:
Decision point, after both calls. Compare on: (a) does the schedule actually work for evenings/weekends, (b) real total price, (c) did they ask you about his body language and threshold distance rather than just selling a package, (d) force-free confirmed, (e) start date — sooner matters, he's 14 months old and this behaviour is currently being rehearsed on every walk.

Default recommendation if the calls are a wash: Orion's $395 6-week reactive class, because it's a real published price, it's built for exactly this problem, it's small enough to stay under threshold, and it comes with homework you can run alongside the week 1-4 plan.

Start the week 1-4 plan immediately regardless of when the class begins — don't wait for a start date to begin the leash mechanics and the sniffaris.
